clinician.final_diagnosis: This female infant demonstrates a case of Bartter syndrome type II with compound heterozygosity for two different pathogenic KCNJ1 gene variants who developed resolution of hyponatremia by 7 weeks of age while the classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis was not seen on follow up.
clinician.trajectory_summary: A premature female infant, born with antenatal polyhydramnios and very low birth weight, presented with poor responsiveness, dehydration, and significant weight loss. By day of life 7, she exhibited severe hyponatremia (121 mmol/L), hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L), and evidence of renal salt wasting (urine sodium 118 mmol/L). Genetic testing confirmed Bartter syndrome type II with compound heterozygosity for two pathogenic KCNJ1 gene variants. Her electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks of age, and supplementation was weaned off by 7 weeks, indicating resolution of hyponatremia. Follow-up venous blood gas at 6 months of age showed a normal pH (7.35) with compensated hypercapnia (pCO2 52 mmHg) and slightly elevated bicarbonate (29 mmol/L), which did not represent a classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

Antenatal history included polyhydramnios and possible duplex collecting system.
At day of life 7, serum sodium was 121 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, and chloride 82 mmol/L.
At day of life 7, urea was 19 mmol/L (high for age) and creatinine was 52 μmol/L (normal for age).
At day of life 7, urine testing revealed high sodium of 118 mmol/L (indicating renal salt wasting), urine potassium of 7 mmol/L, and urine chloride of 94 mmol/L, with an osmolality of 369 mOsm/kg.

Genetic testing confirmed compound heterozygosity for two pathogenic variants in the KCNJ1 gene: a paternally inherited frameshift deletion (p.Glu334Glyfs*35) and a maternally inherited missense variant (p.Pro110Leu).
The patient's electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks of life, and supplementation was gradually weaned off by 7 weeks of life, demonstrating resolution of hyponatremia.
At 6 months of age, venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 52 mmHg, and bicarbonate 29 mmol/L, indicating that classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis was not seen on follow up.
